speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) under what conditions does LTA revoke a Taxi Driver's Vocational Licence (TDVL); and (b) what due process takes place to enable taxi drivers to have a fair hearing before revocation of TDVLs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure in her answer whether she actually touched on what due process the taxi driver has to make representations before his TDVL is revoked by the Land Transport Authority (LTA).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there any direct communication between the driver and LTA, which is the authority that actually has the power to revoke the licence?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Now, from what I know of the facts, the taxi driver disputes the complaint from the passenger.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, the question, of course, will be what protection does the taxi driver have if frivolous or unjust complaints are made against him?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And how does LTA assess the credibility of such a matter and give the taxi driver due hearing before the revocation decision?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When she talked about direct communication between LTA and the taxi drivers whose licences could be revoked, what sort of direct communication does she have in mind?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In 1982, when the decision to revoke taxi drivers' licences was vested in the Registrar of Vehicles (ROV) at the time, the then Minister Ong Teng Cheong, said at that time that the Registrar's decision would be based on evidence adduced from both the complainant and the driver.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I wanted to understand more about the process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: As in the driver's version of events, is that directly communicated or submitted directly to LTA at the first instance, or how does that come about?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: LTA does not revoke a taxi driver's vocational licence without basis.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An important consideration, which LTA must bear in mind in taking its decision, is the risk of the case to potential passenger safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I believe in this case, Ms Lim has done so on behalf of the taxi driver licence holder, whose licence was revoked.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not sure whether I heard the Senior Minister of State correctly, but she mentioned that because now there is an appeal route to the Minister, LTA is reviewing the facts of the case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: My question was: at the first instance when they decide to revoke that licence, what protection do taxi drivers have against frivolous complaints being made against them?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It is a general question not related to that particular case, but a question of policy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, Madam, with your permission, I would just like to share a little bit more about how taxi drivers' licences could be revoked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I mentioned in my reply that there were several conditions that needed to be met.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are not frivolous; in fact, they are also very transparent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the case of a licence being revoked, if demerit points had been accumulated, in many of the cases, the taxi driver could well have experienced periods of suspension.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, before the licence is revoked, quite a number of these taxi drivers would already know that their demerit points are accumulating, so it would not come as a surprise to a lot of them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And what are the reasons where they might accumulate demerit points?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is also made known to every taxi driver.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a transparent list of items – what sorts of conduct will lead to what sorts of demerit points, so there are facts which have led to the accumulation of the demerit points.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it would not be a case of total surprise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Yes, just to clarify again, my question really is premised upon seeking to understand what avenues the taxi driver has to put out his case before LTA makes that decision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Of course, you mentioned this demerit points system and all that —

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: How does LTA assess whether the complaint —

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Please speak one person at a time and address the Chair.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Yes, Madam, I am quite disturbed because I am not refuting the Government's response, but it is just that in the case which I came across, it was not put to the taxi driver that he has accumulated points.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It was just put to him that he has an outstanding case against him.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Is she asking about revocation in general, or she would like to talk about the case that she has encountered?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The case which I encountered actually is an illustration of doubts about what the policy is.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Is it possible for taxi drivers to have their licences revoked just based on one outstanding case?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I do not need to talk about that case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But, in general, just one outstanding case and a case which has not been settled in the Court of law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think we have established from the earlier clarification made by the Member that she is not asking about specific instances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I think those were already in the earlier reply on the general policy.
